summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct under its 2014 Penal Code, which extended the offence beyond Muslims to everyone, and reporting on the statute notes that death-penalty provisions remain theoretically in reach.

Enforcement is documented rather than theoretical. Police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after they were found engaging in homosexual activity in a private home. The prosecution reached into a residence on a local island, so exposure is not confined to public space or to Maldivian nationals; Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats.

The state's international legal position narrows the protection available to a visitor. The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC, and UN review of those reservations records concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage. The Human Rights Committee has recommended that the Maldives adopt anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and take action against the stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Human-rights experts consulted for the HRMI Maldives Summary Report 2024 most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers, as being at risk of empowerment-rights violations. The same survey scores political participation relatively better at 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights score considerably lower, indicating that formal participation rights do not translate into protection for the groups named.
tangentialFactors:
The Maldives' own UPR submission (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015) reports that of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons, and claims full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years. The compilation does not identify which of the accepted recommendations concerned sexual orientation, so the accounting cannot be read as a measure of protection for LGBTQIA+ people.

The gap between the political-participation score of 6.4/10 and the considerably lower scores for other civil and political rights in the 2024 expert survey is the closest available proxy for how the Maldives compares with its own stated commitments: participation is comparatively strong while the rights that would shield a minority from prosecution are not.

The concern recorded in UN review about sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage indicates that religious law shapes outcomes in adjacent personal-status matters, which is context for how a same-sex conduct charge would be framed domestically.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same 2014 Penal Code provisions that reach private homes, as the Dhaandhoo arrests show, and the extension of the offence beyond Muslims means the statute applies across the population rather than to a defined religious group.

The government reports full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 of the first-cycle UPR recommendations over four years, while the Human Rights Committee's recommendation to legislate against discrimination covering sexual orientation and to act against stigmatisation of homosexuals remains on the record.

HRMI's 2024 expert survey places LGBTQIA+ people among the groups most frequently identified as at risk of empowerment-rights violations, with political participation scored at 6.4/10 and other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not address legal gender recognition, gender markers on identity or travel documents, access to gender-affirming care, restroom or facility rules, hate-crime provisions with sexual-orientation aggravation, or recognition of same-sex partners. Whether any of these are governed by separate Maldivian instruments is unresolved here.

Whether the death-penalty provisions noted in reporting on the 2014 Penal Code have ever been imposed for same-sex conduct is not sourced; the inventory records only that they are theoretically in reach.

The inventory does not state whether entry, visa or border screening in the Maldives involves any assessment of gender presentation or sexual orientation, nor whether the UPR recommendations accepted, partially accepted or rejected in the government's April 2015 submission included the Human Rights Committee's sexual-orientation recommendation.
